patient.chief_complaint: Brought in unresponsive after witnessed fall, rhythmic arm movements, history of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease concern — family alarmed by EEG report mentioning 'typical CJD pattern'
patient.history_present_illness: A 67-year-old White female retired teacher was brought to the emergency department by her adult son after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure followed by failure to return to normal consciousness over 90 minutes. She has a 3-month history of rapidly progressive dementia — she went from mild cognitive complaints to being unable to recognize her son and needing full-time care. Her neurologist has been evaluating her for suspected prion disease (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). A brain MRI done 4 weeks ago reportedly showed 'cortical ribboning.' Her neurologist had recently mentioned sporadic CJD was probable per the Paris-Edinburgh criteria. She was not started on any specific treatment (none available for CJD). She takes quetiapine for behavioral symptoms and escitalopram for concurrent depression diagnosed before the dementia. On admission she is unresponsive, making occasional groaning sounds. Her son is very distressed because the previous hospital's EEG was reported as showing 'generalized periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 Hz — typical CJD pattern, highly supportive of prion disease.' The son asks whether the 'seizures' require treatment or whether this is 'just the CJD.' The critical clinical question: are the rhythmic movements true NCSE requiring AED treatment (which could improve quality of life) or are they myoclonic jerks of CJD (which do not respond to AEDs and indicate terminal disease)?

neurological_exam.motor: Intermittent myoclonic jerks of both arms irregularly. No purposeful movement. Extensor posturing bilaterally to noxious stimuli. Diffuse increased tone.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Diffusely brisk reflexes bilaterally. Bilateral Babinski present.
neurological_exam.additional: Known probable sCJD (Paris-Edinburgh criteria). Post-ictal 90 minutes. Groaning sounds only. Myoclonic jerks may represent CJD myoclonus vs superimposed NCSE — EEG required to distinguish.

eeg.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG. Two distinct patterns are identified: 1. Generalised periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) — bilateral synchronous, bifrontal predominance, triphasic morphology, 0.8–1.2 Hz, continuous throughout the recording. 2. Superimposed left temporal focal ictal runs — rhythmic 2–3 Hz sharp waves at T3/T5, 15–30 second duration, recurring every 3–5 minutes; morphologically distinct from the generalised PSWC background. Clinical correlation recommended.

Diffuse cortical volume loss. No hemorrhage or mass lesion. The combination of cortical ribboning and deep gray nuclei signal change constitutes a characteristic pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

Levetiracetam: no significant QTc effect reported in published literature.

results.title: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and EEG characteristics
results.key_finding: Sporadic CJD is characterized by rapid neurological decline. EEG findings include generalised periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) at approximately 1 Hz, reported as a supportive diagnostic criterion in established criteria. DWI cortical ribboning and thalamic/basal ganglia signal change are the characteristic imaging findings. RT-QuIC assay sensitivity and specificity for prion disease have been reported in multiple validation studies. The co-occurrence of focal ictal EEG patterns on a PSWC background has been described in case series.

output.summary: Published literature on sporadic CJD documents clinical diagnostic criteria (including EEG, MRI, and CSF biomarker criteria), RT-QuIC performance characteristics, and the electrographic features of CJD-associated PSWCs versus superimposed ictal patterns. The existence of two coexisting EEG patterns in CJD patients has been described. Antiseizure medication use for intercurrent ictal activity in this population is reported in case series and retrospective cohorts.

results.title: Palliative care in prion disease: clinical features and symptom burden
results.key_finding: Prion disease is uniformly fatal. Published literature describes the symptom burden — including myoclonus, agitation, dyspnea, and altered consciousness — encountered across the disease course. The prevalence of intercurrent complications (including infection and ictal events) in this population and their impact on patient comfort have been reviewed in observational cohorts.

output.summary: Published evidence on palliative care in prion disease describes the natural history of sCJD, symptom prevalence across the disease course, and published experience with symptom management approaches reported in the literature. Goals-of-care frameworks and hospice utilization patterns in this population are described in observational studies.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) with superimposed focal left temporal NCSE on a background of typical CJD periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) — two separate EEG patterns requiring different treatment approaches

differential.diagnosis: NCSE from autoimmune encephalitis mimicking CJD
differential.key_features: RT-QuIC positive (>95% specificity), 14-3-3 positive, DWI cortical ribboning — these together confirm prion disease; autoimmune antibodies negative
Autoimmune panel negative; RT-QuIC positive; cortical ribboning; PSWCs at 1 Hz are classic sCJD, not autoimmune encephalitis
The KEY insight is that TWO patterns coexist: CJD PSWCs + focal left temporal NCSE; levetiracetam trial confirmed differential response — focal NCSE responds to AED while PSWCs remain unchanged

critical_actions: Distinguish CJD PSWCs from superimposed focal NCSE — AED trial with repeat EEG resolves this
RT-QuIC CSF for sCJD confirmation (>95% specificity)
Goals of care family meeting — terminal disease; NCSE treatment is comfort-focused
Check QTc — quetiapine + escitalopram combination carries QTc prolongation risk
Do NOT use succinylcholine, Do NOT intubate without goals-of-care discussion in terminal patient
contraindicated_actions: Aggressive AED escalation targeting CJD PSWCs — these do not respond to AEDs and represent the CJD process itself
Intubation and ICU admission without goals-of-care discussion — terminal disease; aggressive interventions require explicit family consent
Diagnosing all rhythmic movements as CJD without EEG — superimposed NCSE in terminal disease is treatable for comfort
key_reasoning_points: Expert-level distinction: CJD PSWCs and focal NCSE coexist on the same EEG — differential AED response (focal NCSE reduces while PSWCs remain) proves two separate patterns
RT-QuIC has >95% specificity for prion disease — positive result is essentially diagnostic in the appropriate clinical context
CJD PSWCs at 1 Hz are a diagnostic criterion for sCJD — they represent the prion disease process, NOT treatable NCSE; do not escalate AEDs targeting PSWCs
Focal NCSE superimposed on CJD represents a treatable complication worth addressing for quality of life and family comfort (patient appears less distressed)
QTc risk: quetiapine + escitalopram both prolong QTc; levetiracetam is safe to add; monitor ECG in terminal patients receiving these agents

red_herrings.data_point: EEG report: 'generalized periodic sharp wave complexes at 1 Hz — typical CJD pattern'
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude ALL rhythmic EEG activity is CJD and no AED treatment is needed
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CJD PSWCs are present, but additional left focal ictal activity is a SEPARATE pattern representing superimposed NCSE. AED trial with repeat EEG reveals differential response. Both diagnoses coexist.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Decide no treatment is appropriate for any EEG abnormality
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Terminal disease does not mean no treatment. Superimposed NCSE causes additional suffering and reduced awareness — levetiracetam can improve quality of remaining life consistent with comfort-focused goals.
